name: Adam
summary: Adam is the first human, formed from the dust and made in God's image to reflect his rule over creation. His disobedience introduced sin and death into the world, making him the representative head of fallen humanity. The New Testament casts him as a foil to Christ, the 'last Adam,' whose obedience reverses what Adam's sin unleashed.

arc.note: God forms Adam from the ground, breathes life into him, and commissions humanity to bear his image and rule creation. Adam stands as the crown of the creation week, living in unbroken fellowship with God.
Placed in Eden to work and keep it, Adam names the animals and receives Eve, establishing marriage and human community. God gives one prohibition, framing obedience as the path of life.
Deceived by the serpent, Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit, grasping at autonomy from God. Their eyes are opened to shame, and sin fractures the created order.
God pronounces judgment—toil, pain, and death—yet embeds a promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. This 'protoevangelium' becomes the seedbed of all messianic hope.
Driven from the garden and barred from the tree of life, Adam nonetheless fathers a line through which the promise will travel. Death enters human experience, but so does the endurance of hope.

name: Noah
summary: Noah is a righteous man who 'walked with God' amid a world consumed by violence, chosen to preserve life through the great Flood. His obedience in building the ark makes him a model of faith, and the rainbow covenant that follows becomes the first formal covenant in Scripture. The New Testament treats him as both a preacher of righteousness and a type of salvation through judgment.

arc.note: Human wickedness fills the earth, grieving God's heart, yet Noah finds grace in his eyes. He stands as a lone righteous figure in a corrupt generation.
God reveals the coming judgment and commands Noah to build an ark to preserve his family and the animals. Noah does 'all that God commanded,' embodying faith that acts on unseen warnings.
The waters of judgment cover the earth, blotting out all flesh outside the ark. The Flood is both a de-creation and a preservation, sparing a remnant to begin anew.
Emerging into a cleansed world, Noah builds an altar, and God establishes an everlasting covenant, setting the rainbow as its sign. God pledges never again to destroy the earth by flood.
Noah's drunkenness and the shame that follows show that the Flood did not cleanse the human heart. Sin persists even in the redeemed remnant, pointing beyond Noah for a lasting solution.

name: Abraham
summary: Abraham is the founding patriarch of Israel, called out of Ur to become the father of a great nation through whom all peoples would be blessed. His life is the paradigm of faith—believing God's promise of land and offspring against all natural odds. The New Testament makes him the archetype of justification by faith and the father of all who believe.

arc.note: God commands Abram to leave his country and kindred for an unknown land, promising to make him a great nation. Abram obeys, launching the story of redemption that will reach every family on earth.

God repeatedly reaffirms the promise of countless descendants, and Abram 'believed the Lord, and it was counted to him as righteousness.' Faith, not works, becomes the ground of his standing before God.
Impatient for the promised son, Abram and Sarai take matters into their own hands through Hagar. The resulting strife reveals the cost of grasping the promise by human scheming.
God renames him Abraham ('father of a multitude') and seals the covenant with the sign of circumcision. The covenant is confirmed as everlasting, binding God to Abraham's line.
Commanded to sacrifice the son of promise, Abraham obeys, and God provides a ram in Isaac's place. This supreme test of faith foreshadows the Father who would not spare his own Son.

name: Isaac
summary: Isaac is the long-awaited son of promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age as living proof that God keeps his word. Though quieter than his father and son, he is the vital link in the covenant line, receiving and passing on the promises. His near-sacrifice and later blessing of Jacob mark the covenant's continuation into the next generation.

arc.note: Isaac is born to aged parents 'at the time of which God had spoken,' his very name ('he laughs') recalling Sarah's disbelieving laughter turned to joy. He is the miracle that anchors the covenant.
Isaac carries the wood for his own offering and submits as his father raises the knife, until God provides a substitute. His passivity in trust foreshadows the willing self-offering of Christ.
A providentially guided servant brings Rebekah, and Isaac loves her, comforted after his mother's death. The covenant line is secured through this marriage arranged under God's guidance.
During famine God reaffirms to Isaac the very promises given to Abraham, and Isaac builds an altar. He inherits and re-lives his father's covenant walk of faith.

Old and blind, Isaac is deceived into blessing Jacob rather than Esau, yet the blessing stands as God's sovereign choice. The covenant passes to the younger son in a story of human frailty and divine purpose.

name: Jacob
summary: Jacob is the third patriarch, a shrewd 'supplanter' whose life is a long wrestling match with God and with his own deceit. Through years of exile, striving, and eventual brokenness, he is transformed into Israel, the namesake of the twelve tribes. His story shows grace triumphing over manipulation, remaking a schemer into a worshiper.

arc.note: Jacob grasps his brother's birthright and steals his blessing through deception. From the womb he is a heel-grabber, seizing by cunning what God had already promised.
Fleeing Esau's wrath, Jacob dreams of a ladder to heaven and hears God renew the covenant to him personally. Grace meets the fugitive, and he vows the Lord will be his God.
The deceiver is deceived by Laban over marriage and wages, yet God prospers him with family and flocks. Twenty hard years chasten and mature him.
On the eve of meeting Esau, Jacob wrestles a mysterious man until dawn and refuses to let go without a blessing. He is renamed Israel—'he strives with God'—and walks away limping, marked forever.
The brothers meet in tears and embrace, the feared vengeance dissolving into forgiveness. Jacob sees in his brother's face 'the face of God,' the fruit of his transformation.

As an old man in Egypt, Jacob prophetically blesses his twelve sons, foretelling the destiny of the tribes and a ruler from Judah. The supplanter dies a patriarch, entrusting the covenant future to his heirs.

name: Joseph
summary: Joseph is the favored son of Jacob whose dreams of greatness are fulfilled only through betrayal, slavery, and imprisonment. Rising to become Pharaoh's second-in-command, he preserves the family of promise through famine and forgives the brothers who wronged him. His life proclaims the sovereignty of God who works even human evil for good.

arc.note: Loved above his brothers and given a special robe, Joseph dreams that they will bow to him. His favored status and bold dreams provoke deadly jealousy.
His brothers strip and sell him to traders bound for Egypt, faking his death to their father. The dreamer descends into bondage, seemingly abandoned to his enemies.
Joseph prospers as a trusted steward but refuses Potiphar's wife, then is falsely accused and imprisoned. His integrity costs him dearly, yet 'the Lord was with him.'
Even in prison Joseph interprets dreams, crediting God alone, until he is summoned to interpret Pharaoh's. His long wait in the dungeon is not wasted but preparatory.
Elevated to govern all Egypt, Joseph stores grain against seven years of famine. The despised dreamer becomes the savior of nations, his dreams vindicated.
Joseph reveals himself, weeping, and forgives his brothers, declaring that God meant for good what they meant for evil. He preserves the covenant family and models grace toward those who harmed him.

name: Moses
summary: Moses is the towering prophet and lawgiver who led Israel out of Egyptian slavery and mediated the covenant at Sinai. Through him God revealed his name, delivered his people, and gave the Law that shaped Israel's life and worship. Scripture remembers him as uniquely intimate with God, the servant who spoke with the Lord 'face to face,' yet who died within sight of the land he could not enter.

arc.note: Born under a death sentence, Moses is hidden and then drawn from the Nile by Pharaoh's daughter, raised in the very court set to destroy him. God preserves the deliverer within the house of the oppressor.
After killing an Egyptian and fleeing, Moses spends forty years as a shepherd in Midian. The prince becomes a nobody, humbled and prepared for his true calling.
God appears in flame that does not consume, revealing his name 'I AM' and commissioning the reluctant Moses to free Israel. The encounter marks the turning point from exile to mission.
Through ten plagues, Passover, and the parting of the sea, God defeats Egypt and delivers his people. The exodus becomes the defining act of salvation in the Old Testament.
At Sinai God gives the Ten Commandments and covenant law, and Moses's face shines from being in God's presence. Israel is constituted as a holy nation bound to its Redeemer.

Moses leads a grumbling, faithless generation through the desert, interceding for them repeatedly, yet forfeits entry to Canaan through his own disobedience at the rock. His leadership is marked by both patient intercession and human failure.
From Mount Nebo Moses views the land he cannot enter, then dies and is buried by God himself. He passes as the unequaled prophet, awaiting one greater to come.

name: Joshua
summary: Joshua is Moses's faithful successor who led Israel across the Jordan to take possession of the Promised Land. A man of courage and obedience, he is remembered for trusting God's promises when others faltered and for calling the nation to wholehearted service. His name, the Hebrew form of 'Jesus,' points forward to the greater Savior who brings his people into eternal rest.

arc.note: Joshua serves as Moses's assistant and lingers at the tent of meeting, formed for leadership through years of faithful service. He learns to follow before he is called to lead.
Among the twelve spies, only Joshua and Caleb urge Israel to trust God and take the land. His faith stands out against a generation paralyzed by fear.
After Moses's death God charges Joshua to be strong and courageous, promising his presence. The mantle of leadership passes with the assurance that God, not Joshua, secures the victory.
From the fall of Jericho onward, Joshua leads Israel in campaigns that the Lord fights on their behalf. Obedient faith, not military might, wins the land.
Joshua apportions the inheritance among the tribes, and 'not one word of all the good promises' failed. The land-gift fulfills the covenant made to the patriarchs.

In his farewell Joshua summons Israel to choose whom they will serve, declaring, 'As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.' He ends his life calling the nation to decisive, wholehearted loyalty.

name: Deborah
era: Period of the Judges (~12th century BC)
summary: Deborah is a prophetess and the only female judge of Israel, a decisive leader who summoned the nation to war against Canaanite oppression. Sitting under her palm to render judgment, she combined spiritual insight with courageous command. Her victory song is among the oldest poetry in Scripture, celebrating God as the true deliverer of his people.

arc.note: Deborah leads Israel and settles disputes under her palm tree, esteemed as one who speaks for God. In a lawless era, she embodies faithful, God-given authority.
She summons Barak to lead the army against Sisera, going with him when he hesitates and foretelling that the victory's honor will fall to a woman. Her boldness rallies a fearful nation to obedience.
At Deborah's word Israel routs Sisera's army, the Lord throwing the enemy into panic. Deliverance comes as she trusts God's timing and command.
Deborah and Barak sing an exultant hymn crediting the Lord for the triumph and honoring those who volunteered. The song frames the whole episode as worship, giving glory to God alone.

name: Samson
era: Period of the Judges (~11th century BC)
summary: Samson is a Nazirite judge endowed with extraordinary strength to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines. His life is a tragedy of squandered gifting—repeatedly compromised by sensual appetite and pride—yet God works even through his flaws. In his final act, broken and blinded, he achieves his greatest victory, a picture of strength perfected in weakness and grace amid failure.

arc.note: An angel announces Samson's birth to a barren couple, setting him apart as a Nazirite from the womb to begin saving Israel. He is a gift of God with a sacred calling.
The Spirit rushes upon Samson, and he tears a lion and strikes down Philistines single-handedly. His feats display God's power at work despite his volatile character.
Ensnared by his love for Delilah, Samson at last surrenders the secret of his strength. His appetite for what is forbidden repeatedly undoes him.
His hair cut and his strength gone, Samson is seized, blinded, and set to grinding in prison. The mighty judge is reduced to a captive, learning the cost of his compromise.
Praying one last time, Samson pushes down the pillars of Dagon's temple, killing more in his death than in his life. In brokenness he becomes, through sacrifice, an instrument of deliverance.

name: Ruth
era: Period of the Judges (~12th–11th century BC)
summary: Ruth is a Moabite widow whose steadfast loyalty to her mother-in-law Naomi and to Naomi's God makes her a shining example of covenant faithfulness. Gleaning in the fields of Boaz, she is redeemed through marriage and woven into the royal line of David. Her story shows God's grace reaching beyond Israel to draw a Gentile into the lineage of the Messiah.

arc.note: Widowed and free to return home, Ruth clings to Naomi with a vow of unbreaking devotion: 'Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.' Her loyalty is a conversion of both heart and allegiance.
Working the fields to sustain Naomi, Ruth 'happens' upon the field of Boaz, who shows her favor and shelter. God's quiet providence guides her steps toward redemption.
At Naomi's counsel Ruth asks Boaz to spread his cloak over her as redeemer. Her bold request casts herself on covenant kindness rather than on chance.
Boaz redeems Ruth publicly and marries her, and their son Obed becomes the grandfather of David. The foreign widow is grafted into the family through whom the Messiah will come.

name: Samuel
era: End of the Judges / Rise of the Monarchy (~11th century BC)
summary: Samuel is the last judge and first of the great prophets, the bridge between the era of the judges and the monarchy. Dedicated to God from infancy, he leads Israel in revival, anoints its first two kings, and speaks God's word without compromise. He stands as a model of a life wholly given to God and a faithful voice amid national transition.

arc.note: Born in answer to his mother Hannah's desperate prayer, Samuel is 'lent to the Lord' for all his life. His very existence testifies to God who hears and answers.
As a boy serving in the temple, Samuel hears God call and answers, 'Speak, for your servant hears.' The word of the Lord, rare in those days, comes to rest on him.
Samuel leads Israel in repentance and intercession, judging the nation and turning it back to God. He governs with prayer and prophetic authority.
At the people's demand for a king, Samuel reluctantly anoints Saul while warning of monarchy's dangers. He vows never to stop praying for the people, even in his displeasure.
After Saul's rejection, Samuel anoints the young shepherd David, learning that God looks on the heart. His final great act sets the true king on his path.

name: Saul
summary: Saul is Israel's first king, a tall and impressive man chosen to lead the nation yet undone by pride, impatience, and disobedience. Beginning with humility and early victories, he declined into jealousy, paranoia, and open rebellion against God's word. His tragic story is a sober warning that outward advantages cannot substitute for a heart of obedience.

arc.note: Samuel privately anoints Saul at God's direction, and he is later publicly acclaimed. He begins humbly, even hiding among the baggage, seemingly a promising leader.
The Spirit rushes upon Saul, and he rallies Israel to rout the Ammonites and rescue Jabesh-gilead. His reign opens with Spirit-empowered deliverance.
Growing impatient, Saul offers the sacrifice himself rather than wait for Samuel, and is told his kingdom will not endure. His first great failure is unlawful presumption before God.

After sparing what God commanded destroyed and offering excuses, Saul hears that rebellion is as the sin of divination and that God has rejected him as king. Partial obedience is exposed as disobedience.
Consumed by envy of David's success, Saul repeatedly tries to kill him. His paranoia hardens into a long, obsessive pursuit that devours his reign.
Abandoned by God and desperate, Saul seeks out a medium to summon Samuel, only to hear his doom confirmed. His descent into forbidden practices seals his estrangement from the Lord.
Wounded in battle and facing capture, Saul falls on his own sword. The impressive king dies in defeat, a monument to the ruin of a divided heart.

name: David
summary: David is Israel's greatest king, a shepherd anointed in obscurity who became a warrior, poet, and 'man after God's own heart.' His reign united the nation and established Jerusalem as its spiritual center, while God covenanted an everlasting dynasty through his line. Though he sinned grievously, his heartfelt repentance and lifelong worship make him the model of a faith that clings to God's mercy—and the ancestor and pattern of the Messiah.

arc.note: The youngest son, overlooked by his family, is anointed by Samuel as the Spirit rushes upon him. God chooses the shepherd's heart over outward appearance.
David faces the giant in the name of the Lord of hosts, trusting that 'the battle is the Lord's.' His faith-driven victory launches him into public life.
Hunted by Saul, David refuses to harm 'the Lord's anointed,' waiting on God rather than seizing the throne. His restraint and psalms of these years reveal deep trust under pressure.
Crowned over the united nation, David captures Jerusalem, and God covenants an everlasting throne to his offspring. The Davidic covenant becomes the backbone of messianic hope.
David commits adultery and engineers Uriah's death, then is confronted by Nathan and confesses, 'I have sinned against the Lord.' His fall and honest repentance define his relationship with grace.
David flees his own son's uprising and weeps bitterly at Absalom's death. He reaps painful consequences even under forgiveness, bearing sorrow with a submissive heart.
Forbidden to build the temple himself, David gathers materials and charges Solomon, ending his life in exuberant praise. He passes on a legacy of worship centered on the God he loved.

name: Solomon
summary: Solomon is David's son and successor, famed for the wisdom he requested from God and the magnificent temple he built in Jerusalem. His reign marked the zenith of Israel's wealth, peace, and international influence. Yet his heart was gradually turned by wealth and foreign wives toward idolatry, and after his death the kingdom split—a cautionary arc from glory to compromise.

arc.note: Offered anything by God, Solomon asks for an understanding heart to govern, and is granted wisdom, riches, and honor besides. His humble request marks the high point of his devotion.
Solomon constructs the temple as a permanent dwelling for God's name, and the glory-cloud fills it at completion. He gives Israel its central place of worship.
Solomon prays that God would hear his people whenever they turn toward the temple in repentance. The prayer expresses a mature theology of grace and forgiveness.
Solomon surpasses all kings in riches and wisdom, drawing rulers like the queen of Sheba from afar. Israel enjoys unrivaled peace and prosperity.
His many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods, and he builds high places for their worship. The wisest of kings is undone by divided loyalty.
In judgment God announces the kingdom will be torn from Solomon's son, leaving only one tribe for David's sake. His compromise sows the seeds of national division.

name: Elijah
era: Divided Kingdom / Northern Israel (~9th century BC)
summary: Elijah is the fiery prophet who confronted Israel's idolatry under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, calling the nation back to the Lord. His ministry blazed with dramatic signs—drought, fire from heaven, and being fed by ravens—yet also knew deep despair. Taken to heaven in a whirlwind, he became the archetypal prophet, expected to return before the great day of the Lord.

arc.note: Elijah abruptly appears before Ahab, declaring a drought at his word until the Lord relents. He confronts Baal, the supposed storm-god, at the point of his claimed power.
God sustains Elijah by ravens and then by a widow's unfailing jar of flour and oil. In the famine God provides for his prophet and for those who trust him.
In a contest with the prophets of Baal, Elijah prays and fire falls from heaven, and the people cry, 'The Lord, he is God!' The showdown vindicates the Lord as the only true God.
Fleeing Jezebel's death threat, the exhausted prophet collapses and asks to die. Even a mighty man of God knows crushing fear and depression.
At Horeb God passes by not in wind, earthquake, or fire but in a gentle whisper, gently recommissioning Elijah. God meets the despairing prophet with tenderness and renewed purpose.
Elijah calls Elisha to succeed him, casting his cloak upon him. His ministry is entrusted to another, ensuring continuity of God's word.
Elijah is carried up by a whirlwind in a chariot of fire, never seeing death. His extraordinary departure marks him as the prophet par excellence.

name: Elisha
era: Divided Kingdom / Northern Israel (~9th–8th century BC)
summary: Elisha is Elijah's successor who asked for and received a 'double portion' of his master's spirit, ministering for decades in Israel. His ministry abounded in miracles of provision, healing, and life, showing God's compassionate power among ordinary people and foreign strangers alike. He embodies faithful continuation—a servant who carried forward the prophetic mission with grace and wonder.

arc.note: Elisha refuses to leave Elijah and receives a double portion of his spirit, then parts the Jordan with the fallen cloak. The prophetic office passes on with divine confirmation.
Elisha multiplies a widow's oil and feeds a hundred men with limited bread. His ministry displays God's care for the poor and hungry.
Elisha restores a dead child to life through fervent prayer and personal engagement. God's power over death breaks into the life of a faithful household.
The Syrian commander is cleansed of leprosy after humbling himself to wash in the Jordan. God's mercy reaches beyond Israel to a Gentile who obeys in faith.
Even after death, contact with Elisha's bones raises a dead man to life. The prophet's life and death alike testify to the life-giving power of God.

name: Jeroboam
summary: Jeroboam is the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the split from Judah, raised up by God as judgment on Solomon's house. Fearing his people would return to Jerusalem, he established rival worship with golden calves at Bethel and Dan. He becomes the Bible's byword for leading a nation into sin, the pattern by which later northern kings are condemned.

arc.note: The prophet Ahijah tears his garment into twelve pieces, giving Jeroboam ten tribes as God's judgment on Solomon. He is given the kingdom with a conditional promise of an enduring dynasty.
When Rehoboam threatens harsher rule, the northern tribes secede and make Jeroboam king. The united kingdom of David and Solomon is torn apart.

Fearing loss of loyalty, Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and invents his own priesthood and festivals. His political idolatry becomes 'the sin of Jeroboam' that stains Israel for generations.
For his sin God pronounces the extinction of Jeroboam's house and the eventual exile of Israel. The king who feared losing his throne forfeits it for his descendants.

name: Asa
summary: Asa is an early king of Judah remembered for his sweeping religious reforms and his great victory won by trusting God against an overwhelming army. For much of his reign he was wholeheartedly devoted to the Lord, removing idols and renewing covenant. Yet in his later years he leaned on political alliances and grew hardened when rebuked—a life of faith marred by a failure to persevere.

arc.note: Asa removes foreign altars and idols and leads Judah into a covenant to seek the Lord wholeheartedly. His early reign is marked by zealous devotion and national renewal.
Facing a vast Ethiopian army, Asa cries out that God alone can help the weak, and the Lord routs the enemy. His crisis-prayer becomes a high point of dependent faith.
Later, threatened by Israel, Asa buys the help of Aram instead of relying on God and is rebuked by the seer Hanani. He responds in anger, imprisoning the prophet—faith giving way to self-reliance.
Diseased in his feet, Asa 'did not seek the Lord, but sought help from physicians,' and later dies. His decline is a sober warning against finishing poorly.

name: Hezekiah
summary: Hezekiah is one of Judah's most faithful kings, who trusted the Lord as no king before or after him and led a great restoration of true worship. When Assyria besieged Jerusalem, he spread the enemy's threatening letter before God and was delivered by a miracle. His reign models prayerful dependence on God in national crisis, though it closed with a lapse of pride.

arc.note: Hezekiah reopens and cleanses the temple, restores worship, and removes the high places, holding fast to the Lord. He reverses the apostasy of his father Ahaz.
The Assyrian field commander taunts Judah and mocks the Lord's ability to save. The nation faces annihilation and blasphemous defiance of God.
Hezekiah spreads the threatening letter before the Lord and prays for rescue, and the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian army. His prayer turns crisis into a display of God's glory.
Told he will die, Hezekiah weeps and prays, and God grants him fifteen more years. His life is extended in answer to earnest, tearful petition.
Hezekiah proudly shows his treasures to Babylonian envoys, prompting Isaiah's prophecy of future exile. A moment of vanity foreshadows the nation's coming judgment.
Hezekiah secures Jerusalem's water by building a tunnel, a lasting monument to his careful stewardship. He leaves a legacy of both faith and practical wisdom.

name: Josiah
summary: Josiah is the boy-king of Judah whose discovery of the lost Book of the Law sparked the last great reformation before the exile. Tearing his robes in grief over the nation's disobedience, he led sweeping reforms and renewed the covenant. Scripture praises him as a king who turned to the Lord with all his heart, yet his early death at Megiddo hastened Judah's decline.

arc.note: Josiah becomes king as a child and 'did what was right in the eyes of the Lord,' walking in David's ways. His reign begins the last hope of reform for a wayward nation.

arc.stage: Discovery of the Book of the Law
arc.note: During temple repairs the Book of the Law is found, and Josiah tears his clothes in grief at how far Judah has strayed. God's rediscovered word cuts him to the heart.
Huldah confirms coming judgment but promises Josiah will be spared it because of his tender, humble heart. His repentance is honored even amid inevitable national judgment.
Josiah renews the covenant and purges idolatry so thoroughly that no king before or after turned to the Lord like him. He obeys 'with all his heart and all his soul.'
Josiah is fatally wounded confronting Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo, and all Judah mourns. The good king's untimely death removes the nation's last godly restraint before exile.

name: Isaiah
summary: Isaiah is the greatest of the writing prophets, whose vision of God's holiness and majestic prophecies span judgment and comfort. Ministering across the reigns of several kings, he called Judah to trust God rather than foreign powers and unveiled the coming Servant who would bear the sins of many. Quoted more than any other prophet in the New Testament, his book is often called the 'fifth Gospel' for its rich foreshadowing of Christ.

arc.note: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, with seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' The overwhelming vision of God's holiness frames his entire ministry.
Undone by his own uncleanness, Isaiah is cleansed by a burning coal and answers the call, 'Here am I! Send me.' Grace prepares the prophet for a hard mission.

arc.stage: Prophecy amid the Reign of Kings
arc.note: Amid political crisis Isaiah announces signs of Immanuel and a child who will reign on David's throne forever. His words point beyond present kings to the promised Messiah.
Isaiah unveils the Suffering Servant who is pierced for our transgressions and bears the iniquity of us all. These songs offer the clearest Old Testament portrait of the atoning Messiah.
Looking beyond judgment, Isaiah proclaims comfort, a highway for God, and free grace for the thirsty. He gives Israel enduring hope of restoration and everlasting covenant.

name: Jeremiah
summary: Jeremiah is the 'weeping prophet,' called to proclaim judgment on Judah in the decades before and during the Babylonian conquest. Rejected, imprisoned, and heartbroken, he faithfully spoke God's word amid a hostile people who would not listen. Yet through the ruin he announced a stunning hope: a New Covenant written on the heart, fulfilled ultimately in Christ.

arc.note: God tells Jeremiah he was known and appointed a prophet to the nations before he was formed in the womb. The reluctant young man is assured of God's presence.
Jeremiah warns that trusting in the temple while living unjustly is empty, and calls for genuine repentance. His confrontational preaching earns him hostility and rejection.
Jeremiah pours out anguished complaints to God, feeling deceived and cursing the day of his birth, yet unable to stop speaking God's word. His raw laments reveal the cost of faithful prophecy.
For his message of surrender, Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern to die before being rescued. He suffers as a rejected messenger of an unwelcome truth.
Amid judgment Jeremiah foretells a New Covenant in which God writes his law on hearts and forgives sin. This is one of the Old Testament's brightest gospel promises.
As Jerusalem falls, Jeremiah mourns her devastation yet clings to God's steadfast love, 'new every morning.' His grief is held within enduring hope in God's faithfulness.

name: Ezekiel
summary: Ezekiel is a priest-prophet who ministered to the exiles in Babylon through extraordinary visions and dramatic sign-acts. He proclaimed the departure and eventual return of God's glory, indicted Israel's sin, and promised a new heart and spirit for a restored people. His visions of dry bones and a rebuilt temple gave the exiles hope of resurrection life and God's dwelling among them.

arc.note: By the Chebar canal Ezekiel sees the awesome mobile throne of God, revealing that the Lord's glory is present even in exile. The vision assures the exiles their God has not abandoned them.
Ezekiel is shown the idolatry defiling the temple, and the glory of God departs from it. Judgment falls because God's own house has been profaned.
Ezekiel dramatizes the siege and exile with a model city and packed baggage, embodying his message. His life becomes a living sign to a stubborn people.
Ezekiel pronounces judgment on surrounding nations that gloated over Judah's fall. God's sovereignty extends over all peoples, not Israel alone.
Ezekiel prophesies to a valley of dry bones, which rise and live by God's breath, picturing Israel's national resurrection. Hopeless death is reversed by the Spirit of God.
Ezekiel sees God's glory returning to a new temple, and the city is named 'The Lord Is There.' The vision ends with the promise of God dwelling permanently with his people.

name: Daniel
summary: Daniel is a young Judean exile who rose to prominence in the courts of Babylon and Persia while remaining uncompromisingly faithful to God. Through his integrity, prayer life, and God-given wisdom, he interpreted dreams, survived the lions' den, and received sweeping apocalyptic visions. His life models how to live faithfully under pagan rule and points to the coming everlasting kingdom of God.

arc.note: Daniel and his friends are deported and enrolled in Babylonian training, given new names to reshape their identity. Exile threatens to absorb them into a foreign culture.
Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the king's food, and God blesses his conviction with health and favor. Faithfulness in small things sets the tone for his whole life.

Daniel reveals and interprets the king's dream of a great statue, foretelling successive kingdoms and God's everlasting kingdom. He testifies that the God of heaven, not earthly empires, rules history.
His three friends refuse to worship the golden image and are preserved unharmed in the furnace, joined by a fourth figure. Their defiance shows faith that trusts God whether or not he delivers.
Daniel interprets the mysterious handwriting announcing Babylon's fall to the Medes and Persians that very night. God humbles proud kings who defy him.
Refusing to stop praying, Daniel is thrown to the lions but is shut safe by an angel. His unwavering devotion is vindicated before the whole empire.
Daniel sees 'one like a son of man' given everlasting dominion by the Ancient of Days. His visions unveil God's ultimate triumph and the coming Messianic kingdom.

name: Zerubbabel
summary: Zerubbabel is the Davidic governor who led the first wave of exiles back from Babylon and oversaw the rebuilding of the temple. Facing opposition and discouragement, he persevered with the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urging the work on. As heir of David featured in Jesus's genealogy, he represents the survival of the messianic line and the renewal of God's presence among his returning people.

arc.note: Zerubbabel leads the first return of exiles to Jerusalem and rebuilds the altar to restore worship. The scattered people begin to reclaim their identity and their God.
The temple foundation is laid amid shouts of joy mingled with the weeping of those who remembered the former temple. Hope and grief meet as the rebuilding begins.
Adversaries and discouragement halt the work for years until Haggai rebukes the people's neglect. Zerubbabel must overcome fear and apathy to press on.
Encouraged that it is 'not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,' Zerubbabel finishes the temple. God's house is restored through Spirit-empowered perseverance.

name: Ezra
summary: Ezra is a priest and scribe 'skilled in the Law of Moses' who led a later return of exiles and devoted himself to teaching God's word. He restored the centrality of Scripture in the life of the restored community and confronted the crisis of intermarriage with pagan peoples. He models a heart 'set to study, to do, and to teach' the Law of the Lord.

arc.note: Ezra travels to Jerusalem with royal backing, having set his heart to study, obey, and teach the Law. He comes as a reformer devoted to God's word.
Ezra reads the Law aloud to the assembled people, who weep and worship as they understand it. The word of God is restored to the center of national life.
Grieved by the people's intermarriage with the surrounding nations, Ezra prays in anguished confession and leads them in painful repentance. He calls the community to costly covenant faithfulness.

name: Nehemiah
summary: Nehemiah is the cupbearer to the Persian king who returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its ruined walls, uniting practical leadership with fervent prayer. Against fierce opposition he mobilized the people to complete the walls in just fifty-two days. He exemplifies the marriage of dependence on God and diligent, courageous action.

arc.note: Hearing of Jerusalem's broken walls, Nehemiah weeps and prays, then boldly asks the king for permission to rebuild. His grief becomes intercession and then decisive action.
Nehemiah confesses the nation's sin and appeals to God's covenant promises before undertaking his mission. He grounds his bold plans in humble reliance on God.

Organizing the people to build with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, Nehemiah sees the walls finished in fifty-two days. The swift work testifies that 'this had been accomplished with the help of our God.'
Sanballat and Tobiah use ridicule, threats, and plots to stop the work, but Nehemiah answers with prayer and vigilance. He refuses to be intimidated or distracted from his God-given task.
After the walls are done, the people bind themselves in a solemn covenant to obey God's law. Physical restoration is completed by spiritual recommitment.

name: Zechariah
summary: Zechariah is a post-exilic prophet who encouraged the returned community to rebuild the temple and lifted their eyes to the coming Messiah. Through a series of night visions and oracles, he unveiled God's plans to cleanse his people and dwell among them. His book is intensely messianic, foretelling the humble king on a donkey and the pierced shepherd fulfilled in Christ.

arc.note: Zechariah receives a sequence of visions assuring that God will return to Jerusalem in mercy. The visions rekindle hope in a discouraged community.
Four chariots patrol the earth at God's command, declaring his sovereign oversight of the nations. God rules history and will bring his purposes to pass.
The high priest Joshua is stripped of filthy garments and clothed in clean robes, picturing forgiveness and restoration. God removes the guilt of his people in a single day.
Zechariah foretells a coming servant, the 'Branch,' who will be both priest and king and build the true temple. The hope of the community is anchored in a Messianic figure.
Zechariah announces the humble king coming on a donkey and one who is pierced, whom the people will mourn. These oracles find striking fulfillment in the life and death of Jesus.

name: John the Baptist
summary: John the Baptist is the last of the Old Testament–style prophets and the forerunner who prepared the way for Jesus. Living austerely in the wilderness, he preached repentance, baptized the crowds, and pointed to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God.' Jesus called him the greatest born of women, and his fearless witness led to imprisonment and martyrdom under Herod.

arc.note: Born to the aged and barren Elizabeth and Zechariah, John is announced by an angel as one who will go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah. His birth signals the dawn of salvation history's climax.
John lives in the wilderness and appears preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's 'voice crying in the wilderness.' He calls a nation to prepare its heart for the coming Lord.
Crowds come to be baptized in confession of sin, and John baptizes Jesus himself, at which the Spirit descends and the Father speaks. His ministry of preparation reaches its high point.
John identifies Jesus as 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' and gladly decreases so Christ may increase. He models the humility of a true forerunner.
Imprisoned by Herod, John sends to ask whether Jesus is truly the Coming One, and Jesus points to his works as proof. Even the great prophet wrestles with doubt in the darkness.
John is executed to satisfy Herodias's grudge after Herod's rash oath. He dies a martyr for his uncompromising stand for righteousness.

name: Mary (Mother of Jesus)
summary: Mary is the young woman of Nazareth chosen to bear the Son of God, whose humble faith made her the mother of the Messiah. From the annunciation to the cross, she pondered God's works and followed her son through joy and piercing sorrow. She stands as a model of faithful surrender—'Let it be to me according to your word'—and of quiet perseverance in discipleship.

arc.note: The angel Gabriel announces that Mary will conceive by the Holy Spirit, and she answers, 'Let it be to me according to your word.' Her humble consent opens the way for the incarnation.
Mary bursts into praise, magnifying God who lifts the humble and fills the hungry. Her song reveals deep faith and a heart steeped in Scripture.

arc.stage: The Birth of Jesus & Temple Presentation
arc.note: Mary gives birth in Bethlehem and treasures the shepherds' words, then hears Simeon foretell that a sword will pierce her own soul. Joy is intertwined with a warning of coming grief.

arc.stage: The Boy Jesus at the Temple
arc.note: Mary and Joseph find the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple, and Mary 'treasured up all these things in her heart.' She ponders her son's identity as it gradually unfolds.
Mary brings the wine shortage to Jesus and tells the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.' She points others to trust and obey her son.

arc.stage: At the Cross & the Upper Room
arc.note: Mary stands by the cross and is entrusted to the beloved disciple, then joins the praying community after the resurrection. Her faith endures through the sword of grief into the birth of the church.

name: Peter
summary: Peter is the impulsive fisherman who became the leading apostle and spokesman of the early church. Bold yet fallible, he confessed Jesus as the Christ, then denied him, and was restored to shepherd the flock. Transformed by the resurrection and Pentecost, he preached the gospel to Jew and Gentile alike and wrote to encourage suffering believers—a portrait of grace remaking a flawed man into a rock.

arc.note: Jesus calls Peter from his nets to become a fisher of men, and he leaves everything to follow. An ordinary fisherman is drawn into extraordinary purpose.
Peter confesses Jesus as 'the Christ, the Son of the living God,' and is told he is the rock on which the church will be built. His faith is honored even as he still has much to learn.
Under pressure Peter denies knowing Jesus three times, then weeps bitterly at the crowing rooster. His confidence collapses in his darkest failure.
The risen Jesus asks Peter three times, 'Do you love me?' and recommissions him to feed his sheep. Grace restores and re-entrusts the fallen disciple.
Filled with the Spirit, Peter preaches at Pentecost and later opens the gospel to Gentiles at Cornelius's house. The restored apostle becomes a fearless leader of the mission.
Writing to scattered, persecuted believers, Peter urges them to stand firm in living hope and to shepherd God's flock. He turns his hard-won wisdom into pastoral encouragement.

name: Paul
summary: Paul is the former persecutor of the church who, after encountering the risen Christ, became the greatest missionary and theologian of the early church. Through three missionary journeys and thirteen letters, he carried the gospel across the Roman world and articulated the doctrine of justification by faith. His life shows the radical power of grace to transform an enemy of Christ into his most tireless apostle.

arc.note: Zealous for the law, Saul approves of Stephen's death and ravages the church. He is a devout and dangerous enemy of the gospel.
The risen Christ confronts Saul in blinding light, and he is transformed into a chosen instrument to bear Jesus's name to the Gentiles. Grace overturns the persecutor in a moment.
After time apart and early preaching, Paul is cautiously received by the apostles through Barnabas's advocacy. The new convert is gradually woven into the fellowship he once attacked.
Sent out by the Spirit, Paul plants churches across Asia Minor and Greece over three journeys. He becomes the great apostle to the Gentiles, establishing communities of faith far and wide.
Arrested in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar and preaches boldly even under house arrest in Rome. His chains become a platform for the advance of the gospel.

Paul's epistles proclaim justification by faith and shape Christian theology for all time, ending with the confidence that he has 'fought the good fight.' His written legacy outlasts his life and forms the church.

name: Barnabas
summary: Barnabas, whose name means 'son of encouragement,' is a generous and warmhearted leader in the early church who repeatedly opened doors for others. He vouched for the newly converted Paul, nurtured the Antioch church, and partnered in the first missionary journey. His willingness to give a second chance—even to John Mark—makes him a model of encouraging, reconciling ministry.

arc.note: Barnabas sells a field and lays the proceeds at the apostles' feet, earning his name 'son of encouragement.' Generosity marks him from the start.
When the church fears the newly converted Saul, Barnabas takes him in and brings him to the apostles. His trust unlocks Paul's place in the church.
Sent to the growing church in Antioch, Barnabas rejoices at God's grace and recruits Paul to help teach. He builds up a flourishing, mixed community of believers.
Set apart with Paul by the Spirit, Barnabas travels to plant churches and endures hardship for the gospel. He shares in the pioneering mission to the Gentiles.
Barnabas insists on giving John Mark a second chance, parting ways with Paul over the disagreement. His grace toward a failing young worker helps restore Mark to useful service.

name: Timothy
summary: Timothy is Paul's beloved younger protégé and 'true child in the faith,' a faithful coworker in the gospel mission. Raised in Scripture by his mother and grandmother, he was recruited by Paul and entrusted with important pastoral responsibilities. Though timid by nature, he was repeatedly urged to be bold, embodying the passing of the faith to a new generation of leaders.

arc.note: Timothy, of mixed Jewish-Greek heritage and taught the Scriptures from childhood, is well spoken of and chosen by Paul as a companion. His sincere faith is nurtured from an early age.
Paul has Timothy circumcised so as not to needlessly hinder the mission among the Jews. He learns to set aside personal liberty for the sake of the gospel.
Timothy is sent as Paul's trusted representative and is named as co-sender of several letters. He proves himself as one who genuinely cares for the churches.
Paul leaves Timothy to lead the Ephesian church and correct false teaching, urging him not to let others despise his youth. He is entrusted with weighty pastoral leadership.
Paul stirs up Timothy to fan his gift into flame, not to be ashamed of the gospel, and to endure hardship as a good soldier. The timid disciple is called to courageous perseverance.
